title: Assessing mental state, cognition and distress
blurb: Spot people at risk of delirium, use the 4AT, recognise hypoactive delirium and respond to distress, anxiety and agitation safely.
question: Mrs Hughes, 82, is two days after surgery for a hip fracture. Her daughter says she is 'not herself': quieter, muddled about the day and not eating. Staff describe her as no trouble. What should the nurse do?

teach.body: Cognition is how we think, remember, pay attention and make sense of the world. Delirium is a recent change, over hours or days, in thinking, perception, physical function or behaviour, which often fluctuates. Dementia develops gradually. Distress behaviour, such as agitation, shouting or withdrawal, is often a way of communicating an unmet need such as pain, fear or thirst. Plain English: when someone changes quickly, ask what has changed in their body or surroundings, not just in their mind.

teach.h: Who is at risk of delirium? (NICE CG103 rec 1.2.1)
head: Risk factor
Example
rows: Any older person admitted to hospital or care
Deteriorating or at risk of deteriorating
teach.caption: Assess on first presentation to hospital or long-term care. Any one factor means the person is at risk. Keep observing for changes in these factors.

teach.h: Indicators of delirium: recent changes in

cells.label: Restless, immobile, off food, poor sleep

teach.caption: NICE CG103 recs 1.3.1 and 1.5.1: observe people in hospital or long-term care at least daily, and listen to what relatives and carers report.

teach.h: Hypoactive delirium is the one that gets missed
teach.body: Delirium can be hyperactive (restless, agitated) or hypoactive (quiet). NICE CG103 warns to be particularly vigilant for withdrawal, slow responses, reduced mobility and movement, worse concentration and reduced appetite, because these are often mistaken for tiredness, low mood or being 'settled'. If any change is present, assess with the 4AT and document it in the record.

head: Item
What you do
Score
rows: Age, date of birth, place, current year
Change over last 2 weeks, still present in last 24 h
teach.caption: Use the 4AT on wards and in the community. In critical care or recovery use CAM-ICU or ICDSC instead (NICE CG103 rec 1.6.1).

rows.label: If unsure
values: Delirium can sit on top of it

teach.caption: NICE CG103 rec 1.6.3. A delirium-positive 4AT is not a diagnosis: a competent healthcare professional makes the final diagnosis.

steps.label: Look for causes
steps.sub: Pain (including non-verbal signs), hypoxia, infection, thirst, constipation, medicines

steps.label: Communicate
steps.sub: Explain where they are, who they are, your role; involve family

steps.label: If still at risk
steps.sub: Prescriber may consider short-term haloperidol (usually 1 week or less)

teach.caption: NICE CG103 recs 1.4.9, 1.7.2, 1.7.3 (de-escalate first), 1.7.4. Start at the lowest dose and take account of MHRA cautions in older people.

teach.h: Worked example: Mrs Hughes on the orthopaedic ward
items: Risk: she is over 65 and has a current hip fracture, so she was at risk of delirium from admission.
Indicators: her daughter reports a recent change: quieter, muddled, eating little. These fit hypoactive delirium.
4AT: alertness normal (0); AMT4 two mistakes (2); months backwards, five correct (1); acute change, yes (4). Total 7: possible delirium.
The nurse documents the 4AT and the change, escalates to the doctor, and starts looking for causes: pain, constipation, urinary retention, infection, dehydration, medicines.
She reorientates Mrs Hughes gently, makes sure her glasses and hearing aid are in use, and invites her daughter to visit often.

teach.text: 'Quiet and no trouble' is not reassurance in an older person who has changed. Hypoactive delirium looks like being settled. Also, the 4AT suggests delirium; it does not diagnose it, and it is not the tool for intensive care (use CAM-ICU or ICDSC).

items: CG103 risk factors: 65+, cognitive impairment or dementia, current hip fracture, severe illness.
Watch daily for recent changes in cognition, perception, physical function and behaviour; listen to relatives.
Use the 4AT: 0 unlikely, 1–3 possible cognitive impairment, 4+ possible delirium.
If unsure between delirium and dementia, manage delirium first.
Distress: look for causes, reorientate, de-escalate; short-term haloperidol only if still distressed or at risk.

summary: You can now identify people at risk of delirium, recognise its hyperactive and hypoactive signs, use and score the 4AT, and tell delirium from dementia. You can respond to distress, anxiety and agitation by looking for causes and de-escalating before any medicine is considered.

A.q: On admission to an acute medical unit, which person is at risk of delirium under NICE CG103?
options: Ms Cole, 60, admitted for a planned knee operation
Mrs Fenn, 63, with well-controlled hypertension
Mr Lane, 52, admitted with a hip fracture
Mr Ito, 40, admitted for a planned hernia repair
A.why: A current hip fracture is one of the four CG103 risk factors, whatever the person's age.

whyNot.0: She is under 65, has no cognitive impairment, hip fracture or severe illness; a planned operation alone is not a CG103 risk factor.
whyNot.1: She is under 65 and stable; controlled hypertension is not a CG103 risk factor.
whyNot.3: He is young and well; a planned hernia repair is not a CG103 risk factor.

A.q: In the attention item of the 4AT, what is the person asked to do?
options: Count backwards from 20 to 1
Say the months backwards from December
Spell the word WORLD backwards
Recall three objects after 5 minutes
A.why: The 4AT attention item asks for the months of the year in backwards order starting at December; 7 or more correct scores 0.

whyNot.0: Counting backwards from 20 is used in other screening tools, not in the 4AT.
whyNot.2: Spelling WORLD backwards belongs to other cognitive tests, not the 4AT.
whyNot.3: Three-object recall is not part of the 4AT; item 2 is the AMT4 (age, date of birth, place, year).

A.q: Mr Ross, 81, scores 5 on the 4AT. What does this result suggest?
options: Possible delirium
Cognitive impairment without delirium
No delirium or significant impairment
A confirmed diagnosis of dementia
A.why: A 4AT score of 4 or more suggests delirium; a healthcare professional with the relevant expertise then makes the diagnosis.

whyNot.1: 1–3 suggests cognitive impairment without delirium; 5 is above that band.
whyNot.2: Only a score of 0 suggests delirium and moderate-severe impairment are unlikely.
whyNot.3: The 4AT does not diagnose dementia, and a score of 4+ points towards delirium.

B.q: Mrs Begum, 79, is three days after abdominal surgery. She has become withdrawn, eats little and is slow to answer. Staff note she is 'no trouble'. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Record that she is settled and resting well
Refer her for a routine memory assessment
Encourage rest and review her tomorrow
Assess her for delirium using the 4AT
B.why: These are indicators of hypoactive delirium, which NICE CG103 says is often missed. Any such change should prompt an assessment with the 4AT.

whyNot.0: Recording her as settled risks missing hypoactive delirium.
whyNot.1: A routine memory referral delays assessment of an acute change that may have a treatable cause.
whyNot.2: Waiting until tomorrow leaves a possible delirium unassessed.

B.q: Mr Grant, 88, has mild dementia and has been admitted with a chest infection. Which action is part of the NICE CG103 multicomponent package to prevent delirium?
options: Move him to a quieter bay each night
Give his medicines during sleeping hours
Ensure his glasses and hearing aids are used
Insert a urinary catheter to reduce toilet trips
B.why: CG103 rec 1.4.12: address sensory impairment by making sure hearing and visual aids are available, used and working.

whyNot.0: CG103 says avoid moving people within and between wards or rooms unless absolutely necessary.
whyNot.1: CG103 says schedule medicine rounds to avoid disturbing sleep.
whyNot.3: CG103 says avoid unnecessary catheterisation to reduce infection.

B.q: Mr Moore, 83, has delirium and is distressed, pulling at his cannula and hitting out. Calm verbal and non-verbal de-escalation has not worked. What may the prescriber consider under NICE CG103?
options: Short-term haloperidol, usually 1 week or less
Regular lorazepam continued until discharge
Haloperidol for 4 weeks to prevent relapse
A sedating antihistamine every night
B.why: CG103 rec 1.7.4: if de-escalation is ineffective or inappropriate, consider short-term haloperidol (usually for 1 week or less), starting at the lowest dose and titrating cautiously.

whyNot.1: CG103 names short-term haloperidol, not regular benzodiazepines continued until discharge.
whyNot.2: CG103 advises short-term use, usually 1 week or less, not a 4-week course.
whyNot.3: A sedating antihistamine is not the CG103 option and can worsen confusion.

C.q: Mr Hart, 84, has known dementia. Over the last 2 days he has become much more confused, and the team cannot tell whether his dementia has progressed or he has delirium. What does NICE CG103 advise?
options: Treat it as progression of his dementia
Manage it as delirium first and look for causes
Wait 2 weeks to see whether it settles
Refer him to a memory clinic before acting
C.why: CG103 rec 1.6.3: if there is difficulty distinguishing delirium, dementia or delirium superimposed on dementia, manage the delirium first.

whyNot.0: Assuming progression risks missing a treatable cause of delirium.
whyNot.2: Waiting delays treatment of a possible delirium with a physical cause.
whyNot.3: A memory clinic referral does not address an acute change that needs action now.

C.q: Mrs Shaw, 77, is fully alert. She makes one mistake on the AMT4 and gives four months correctly when counting backwards. Her family report no change over the last 2 weeks. What is her 4AT score and its meaning?
options: 2: delirium unlikely and no impairment
6: suggests possible delirium
2: suggests possible cognitive impairment
3: suggests possible delirium
C.why: Alertness 0 + AMT4 one mistake 1 + attention fewer than 7 months 1 + no acute change 0 = 2. A score of 1–3 suggests cognitive impairment but not delirium.

whyNot.0: The score is 2, but only a score of 0 suggests no impairment.
whyNot.1: 6 would need the acute change item (4 points), which scored 0 here.
whyNot.3: The total is 2, not 3, and scores of 1–3 point to cognitive impairment, not delirium.

C.q: Mrs Evans, 70, was admitted this morning. She is restless and keeps asking when she can go home. Her 4AT is 0. She says she is worried about her dog, alone at home. What is the most appropriate initial intervention?
options: Ask the doctor to prescribe a sedative for her
Reassure her that all will be fine and move on
Repeat the 4AT in one hour to recheck her
Listen and help her arrange care for the dog
C.why: Her restlessness has an identifiable cause: anxiety about her dog. Listening and resolving the concern is the person-centred first intervention for anxiety (NMC proficiency P4.8).

whyNot.0: Medication is not a first response to understandable anxiety with a clear cause.
whyNot.1: Brushing aside her concern does not address the cause of her distress.
whyNot.2: Her 4AT is 0; repeating it does not respond to the worry she has told you about.

reteach.title: Change is the clue
reteach.question: Forget the label for a moment. What matters most when an older person seems confused or unusually quiet?

blocks.body: Delirium is about recent change: hours or days, often fluctuating, often reported by family first. A quiet, withdrawn person who has stopped eating may be just as unwell as someone shouting and pulling at lines. When something has changed, use the 4AT, then look for the physical cause.

blocks.text: The 4AT 'acute change' item looks back 2 weeks and needs the change to be evident in the last 24 hours: it scores 4 on its own.

explain.body: NICE CG103 lists four: age 65 or older; cognitive impairment or dementia (past or present); current hip fracture; severe illness (deteriorating or at risk of deterioration).

test.q: Which of these is one of the four NICE CG103 delirium risk factors?
options: Living alone at home
A current hip fracture
A history of depression
Taking four or more medicines
test.why: The four factors are 65 or older, cognitive impairment or dementia, current hip fracture and severe illness.

whyNot.0: Living alone is not one of the four CG103 risk factors.
whyNot.2: Depression is not listed among the four CG103 risk factors.
whyNot.3: Polypharmacy prompts a medication review in prevention, but it is not one of the four risk factors.

explain.body: Recent changes in cognition (poor concentration, slow responses), perception (hallucinations), physical function (restlessness, reduced mobility, appetite, sleep) or social behaviour (withdrawal, mood). Hypoactive signs are often missed.

test.q: Which recent change is an indicator of hypoactive delirium?
options: Reduced appetite and slow responses
Pacing the ward and shouting loudly
Pulling repeatedly at a cannula
Trying again and again to leave
test.why: CG103 lists withdrawal, slow responses, reduced mobility, worse concentration and reduced appetite as signs of hypoactive delirium.

whyNot.1: Pacing and shouting are hyperactive features.
whyNot.2: Pulling at lines is a hyperactive feature.
whyNot.3: Repeated attempts to leave reflect restlessness, a hyperactive feature.

explain.body: Four items: alertness (0 or 4), AMT4 (0–2), attention by months backwards (0–2) and acute change or fluctuation over the last 2 weeks (0 or 4). Total 0–12; 4 or more suggests delirium.

test.q: In the 4AT, over what period is evidence of acute change or fluctuation considered?
options: The last 6 months
The last 2 weeks
The last 4 hours
The last 24 hours
test.why: Item 4 scores a significant change in alertness, cognition or other mental function arising over the last 2 weeks and still evident in the last 24 hours.

whyNot.0: Six months describes a gradual change more typical of dementia.
whyNot.2: Four hours is too short; the 4AT looks back 2 weeks.
whyNot.3: The change must still be evident in the last 24 hours, but it may have arisen at any time over the last 2 weeks.

explain.body: Find causes (pain, infection, hypoxia, dehydration, constipation, medicines, sensory loss). Reorientate: explain where the person is, who they are and your role, and involve family. De-escalate before any medicine is considered.

test.q: According to NICE CG103, how should staff reorientate a person with delirium?
options: Correct each mistaken belief firmly and clearly
Explain where they are, who they are and your role
Limit family visits to reduce overstimulation
Keep the lights low throughout the whole day
test.why: CG103 recs 1.4.4 and 1.7.2: reorientate by explaining where the person is, who they are and what your role is, provide reassurance and involve family and friends.

whyNot.0: Firm correction can increase distress; CG103 describes calm reorientation and reassurance.
whyNot.2: CG103 encourages regular visits from family and friends.
whyNot.3: CG103 recommends appropriate lighting and clear signage, not dim daytime lighting.
